skill.name: concept-to-story
skill.description: Turn abstract concepts in a user-provided book PDF, paper, textbook, lecture note, or long document into source-grounded stories, visual memory anchors, real-life signals, and active recall. Use for learning a chapter, understanding confusing ideas, remembering concepts, or continuing these lessons. Do not select for summary-only requests, book recommendations, shopping, author lookup, or file conversion.
skill.summary: Transform source material into accurate stories, memory anchors, concept maps, and active-recall lessons.
skill.author: autoloading8822

content.value_statement: Dense source material can make abstract ideas difficult to understand and remember. This skill creates faithful stories, visual anchors, concept maps, and recall questions.
actual_capabilities: Builds chapter maps and book maps from verified source material.
Explains one concept through a concrete fictional scene and explicit theory mapping.
Creates short visual memory anchors tied to each concept's mechanism.
Identifies analogy limits, source conditions, and observable real-life signals.
Asks active-recall and transfer questions without revealing answers prematurely.
Produces checkpoints for pausing or continuing an interactive lesson.
limitations: Requires the relevant document or passage to support source-grounded claims.
Does not guarantee memory improvement or independently track long-term retention.
Cannot establish printed page numbers when the source lacks reliable labels.
Stories illustrate concepts but do not replace evidence, proofs, or expert review.

use_cases.title: Study a difficult textbook chapter
use_cases.description: Map the chapter, learn each concept through a faithful story, and test understanding with active recall.

use_cases.title: Prepare a source-grounded lesson
use_cases.description: Convert selected readings into structured explanations, analogy boundaries, and transfer questions for guided instruction.

use_cases.title: Understand a technical paper
use_cases.description: Trace claims to passages while preserving methods, assumptions, notation, and limits in a concrete explanation.

prompt_templates.title: Explain one concept
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the attached document to teach {concept}. Cite the verified passage, create one story and memory anchor, then ask one recall question.
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner lesson focused on a single concept

prompt_templates.title: Map a chapter
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a concept map for {chapter}. Show dependencies among three to seven verified concepts, then teach the first concept.
prompt_templates.scenario: Structured study of a bounded chapter

prompt_templates.title: Resume and test understanding
prompt_templates.prompt: Resume from this checkpoint: {checkpoint}. Review the pending concept, evaluate my answer, and give one transfer question when understanding is demonstrated.
prompt_templates.scenario: Intermediate continuation of an interactive lesson

prompt_templates.title: Analyze a complex technical claim
prompt_templates.prompt: Teach {claim} from {source scope}. Preserve definitions, assumptions, and notation. Use a worked situation when analogy would distort the mechanism.
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced analysis of mathematical, scientific, or technical material

output_examples.input: Teach opportunity cost from the attached economics chapter.
output_examples.output: The lesson cites the verified section, follows a student choosing between two commitments, and maps the sacrifice to the concept. It ends with one new decision scenario.

output_examples.input: Create a map of this chapter on database transactions.
output: A chapter map separates atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability.
Dependency notes identify which ideas rely on transaction boundaries and failure assumptions.
The first lesson uses a concrete transaction failure and asks one recall question.

output_examples.input: Help me remember correlation versus causation from this paper.
output_examples.output: A fictional scene contrasts two linked observations with an untested causal claim. The boundary section preserves the study design limits and possible confounders.

best_practices: Provide the exact document and identify the chapter, pages, or concept you want to study.
Answer each recall question before requesting the next lesson or transfer test.
Ask for a checkpoint when pausing a long learning sequence.
anti_patterns: Do not request source-grounded teaching without providing the source or relevant passage.
Do not treat fictional stories as evidence that a claim is true.
Do not assume an analogy captures every condition, exception, or technical detail.

faq.question: What source formats can I use?
faq.answer: You can provide PDFs, papers, textbooks, lecture notes, long documents, or selected passages.

faq.question: Can it teach an entire book at once?
faq.answer: It first creates a book map, proposes a starting concept, and waits before delivering detailed lessons.

faq.question: How does it prevent invented source claims?
faq.answer: It verifies passages, labels source-derived claims, marks uncertainty, and separates fictional teaching material from source evidence.

faq.question: Does it reveal recall answers immediately?
faq.answer: No. It waits for your response unless you explicitly request the answer.

faq.question: Can it handle equations and technical mechanisms?
faq.answer: Yes. It preserves definitions, variables, assumptions, and exact relations while using stories only when they remain accurate.

faq.question: Does it create images or track my progress?
faq.answer: It creates text-based visual anchors. It uses conversation context and only saves a checkpoint file when requested.
